skills.name: Electronic configuration and chemical properties: alkaline earth metals and halogens

note.text:
Alkaline earth metals (group II: Be, Mg, Ca) have 2 valence electrons and lose both to form +2 ions (Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺).
• Harder and less reactive than group I. Reactivity increases down the group: Ca > Mg > Be.
• Calcium reacts steadily with cold water: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂. Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water but burns in steam and with a bright white flame in air: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.
With halogens they form halides with formula MX₂: Mg + Cl₂ → MgCl₂ (one Mg²⁺ for two Cl⁻).
Their oxides and hydroxides are basic; calcium hydroxide solution is limewater.

sections.heading: Group II: the alkaline earth metals
sections.text:
Beryllium, magnesium and calcium have {2} outer electrons. They react by losing both to form ions with a +{2} charge: Mg → Mg²⁺ + {2}e⁻.
Losing two electrons takes more energy than losing one, so they are less reactive than the alkali metals next to them. They are also harder and denser.

sections.heading: How they react
sections.text:
• With water: calcium fizzes steadily in cold water, giving calcium hydroxide and hydrogen; magnesium reacts only very slowly with cold water but quickly with steam.
• With air: magnesium ribbon burns with a dazzling white flame, forming white magnesium oxide.
• Reactivity increases down the group: beryllium < magnesium < calcium.
Calcium hydroxide solution is limewater, used to test for carbon dioxide.

sections.heading: With halogens
sections.text:
Group II metals react with halogens to form salts. One M²⁺ ion needs two halide ions (each −{1}) to balance its charge, so the formula is MX₂: MgCl₂, CaF₂, CaCl₂.
The halogens behave as in the last lesson: they gain one electron each, and fluorine is the most reactive.

key_words.meaning: a metal oxide that neutralises acids

mistake.why: Mg²⁺ carries two positive charges, so it needs two Cl⁻ ions.

worked_example.problem: Write the formula of calcium chloride and explain it.
steps: Calcium is in group II: it loses {2} electrons, forming Ca²⁺.
Chlorine is in group VII: each atom gains {1} electron, forming Cl⁻.

cards.idea: Group II metals lose {2} electrons to form +{2} ions.
Reactivity increases down group II but is less than group I.
example: Calcium reacts with cold water; magnesium hardly.

pick.q: How many valence electrons does calcium have?
What is the configuration of the calcium ion Ca²⁺?
e: That is the atom; the ion has lost two electrons.

pick.q: Which reacts fastest with cold water?
e: Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water.
pick.y: Calcium is lowest of the three in group II.

pick.r: with a very bright white flame, forming magnesium oxide
w: with a green flame forming magnesium chloride

pick.q: Calcium reacts with water. What are the products?
e: The gas is hydrogen; the hydroxide forms in water.
Calcium carbonate is chalk; it is insoluble.
pick.y: Ca(OH)₂ in water; it turns milky with carbon dioxide.

pick.q: Are the oxides of group II metals acidic or basic?
e: They react with acids, so they are not neutral.
pick.y: MgO and CaO are bases; they neutralise acids.

pick.q: Why is calcium less reactive than potassium, although both are in period 4?
pick.r: Calcium must lose two electrons, which needs more energy than losing one
e: Calcium has more protons (20) than potassium (19).
pick.y: Removing two electrons is harder, and calcium's nucleus holds them more strongly.

pick.q: Strontium is below calcium in group II. How does it react with water?
e: It is lower in the group, so more reactive.
Group II metals react with water.

pick.q: Magnesium burns in chlorine. What is the formula of the product?
e: One Mg²⁺ and two Cl⁻, not two Mg.
Each chloride ion is −1, so only two are needed.
